claim: The ventral occipito-temporal cortex (VOTC) reliably encodes auditory categories in people born blind using a representational structure partially similar to the one found in vision.
source: The ventral occipito-temporal cortex (VOTC) reliably encodes auditory categories in people born blind using a representational structure partially similar to the one found in vision (Mattioni et al.,2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mattioni et al., 2020

claim: Early and late acquired blindness result in enhanced univariate response to sounds in part of the occipital cortex.
source: First, we show enhanced univariate response to sounds in part of the occipital cortex of both blind groups that is concomitant to reduced auditory responses in temporal regions.
evidence: Supported by experimental fMRI data presented in the manuscript

claim: Early and late acquired blindness result in reduced auditory responses in temporal regions.
source: First, we show enhanced univariate response to sounds in part of the occipital cortex of both blind groups that is concomitant to reduced auditory responses in temporal regions.
evidence: Supported by experimental fMRI data presented in the manuscript

claim: The representation of sound categories in occipital and temporal regions is more similar in blind subjects compared to sighted subjects.
source: We then reveal that the representation of the sound categories in the occipital and temporal regions is more similar in blind subjects compared to sighted subjects.
evidence: Supported by RSA analysis presented in the manuscript

claim: The multivoxel encoding of the 'human voice' category observed in the temporal cortex of all sighted and blind groups is enhanced in occipital regions in blind groups.
source: The multivoxel encoding of the 'human voice' category that we observed in the temporal cortex of all sighted and blind groups is enhanced in occipital regions in blind groups
evidence: Supported by MVPA and RSA analyses presented in the manuscript

claim: The representation of vocal information is more similar between the occipital and temporal regions in blind compared to sighted individuals.
source: The multivoxel encoding of the 'human voice' category that we observed in the temporal cortex of all sighted and blind groups is enhanced in occipital regions in blind groups , suggesting that the representation of vocal information is more similar between the occipital and temporal regions in blind compared to sighted individuals.
evidence: Inferred from the enhanced encoding of human voice category in occipital regions of blind groups

claim: Blindness does not affect the encoding of acoustic properties (e.g. pitch, harmonicity) in occipital and temporal regions.
source: We additionally show that blindness does not affect the encoding of the acoustic properties of our sounds (e.g. pitch, harmonicity) in occipital and in temporal regions but instead selectively alter the categorical coding of the voice category itself.
evidence: Supported by RSA analysis with acoustic models presented in the manuscript

claim: Blindness selectively alters the categorical coding of the voice category.
source: We additionally show that blindness does not affect the encoding of the acoustic properties of our sounds (e.g. pitch, harmonicity) in occipital and in temporal regions but instead selectively alter the categorical coding of the voice category itself.
evidence: Supported by RSA analysis with categorical models presented in the manuscript

claim: The occipital cortex of early blind individuals enhances its response to non-visual stimuli.
source: The occipital cortex of early blind (EB) individuals enhances its response to non-visual stimuli (Neville and Bavelier, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Neville and Bavelier, 2002

claim: Sound processing triggers enhanced occipital responses in early blind people.
source: For instance, it has been repetitively shown that sound processing triggers enhanced occipital responses in EB people (Van Ackeren et al., 2018; Bedny et al., 2011; Collignon et al., 2011; Dormal et al., 1981; Weeks et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous studies

claim: Several studies suggested that visual deprivation elicits enhanced response in the sensory cortices responsible for touch or audition.
source: Several studies suggested that visual deprivation elicits enhanced response in the sensory cortices responsible for touch or audition (Elbert et al., 2002; Gougoux et al., 2009; Manjunath et al., 1998; Naveen et al., 1998; Pascual-Leone and Torres, 1993; Rauschecker, 2002; Röder et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous studies

claim: Some studies observed a decreased engagement of auditory or tactile sensory cortices during non-visual processing in early blind individuals.
source: In contrast, some studies observed a decreased engagement of auditory or tactile sensory cortices during non-visual processing in EB individuals (Bedny et al., 2015; Burton et al., 2002; Pietrini et al., 2004; Ricciardi et al., 2009; Stevens and Weaver, 2009; Striem-Amit et al., 2012; Wallmeier et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous studies

claim: A few studies reported an increased representation of auditory stimuli in the occipital cortex concomitant to a decreased auditory representation in temporal regions in congenitally blind people.
source: A few studies reported an increased representation of auditory stimuli in the occipital cortex concomitant to a decreased auditory representation in temporal regions in congenitally blind people (Battal et al., 2021; Dormal et al., 2016; Jiang et al., 2016, van den Hurk et al., 2017; Vetter et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous studies

claim: Categorical membership is the main factor that predicts the representational structure of sounds in ventral occipito-temporal cortex (VOTC) in congenitally blind people, rather than lower-level acoustical attributes of sounds.
source: We have recently demonstrated that categorical membership is the main factor that predicts the representational structure of sounds in ventral occipito-temporal cortex (VOTC) in congenitally blind people (Mattioni et al., 2020), rather than lower-level acoustical attributes of sounds (i.e. pitch).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mattioni et al., 2020

claim: Previous studies suggested that late acquired blindness triggers a reorganization of occipital region that is less functionally organized than the one observed in early blindness.
source: In contrast with this hypothesis, previous studies suggested that late acquired blindness triggers a reorganization of occipital region that is less functionally organized than the one observed in early blindness (Bedny et al., 2012; Collignon et al., 2013; Kanjlia et al., 2009), promoting the idea that crossmodal plasticity in late blindness is more stochastic and functionally epiphenomenal compared to the one observed in EB people.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

source: Importantly, the LB group and the three additional SC subjects were acquired in the same MRI scanner and in the same time period (July 2015–April 2016).
evidence: Describes data acquisition details

claim: The final acoustic stimulus set included 24 sounds from eight different categories (human vocalization, human non-vocalization, birds, mammals, tools, graspable objects, environmental scenes, big mechanical objects).
source: The final acoustic stimulus set included 24 sounds from eight different categories (human vocalization, human non-vocalization, birds, mammals, tools, graspable objects, environmental scenes, big mechanical objects) that could be reduced to four superordinate categories (human, animals, manipulable objects, big objects/places) (see Figure 1 and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Describes the stimulus set used in the experiment

claim: The eight sound categories could be reduced to four superordinate categories (human, animals, manipulable objects, big objects/places).
source: The final acoustic stimulus set included 24 sounds from eight different categories (human vocalization, human non-vocalization, birds, mammals, tools, graspable objects, environmental scenes, big mechanical objects) that could be reduced to four superordinate categories (human, animals, manipulable objects, big objects/places) (see Figure 1 and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Describes the hierarchical organization of stimulus categories

claim: Visual deprivation may trigger a redeployment mechanism that would reallocate part of the processing typically tagging the preserved senses to the occipital cortex deprived of its most salient visual input.
source: An intriguing possibility raised by our results is that visual deprivation may actually trigger a redeployment mechanism that would reallocate part of the processing typically tagging the preserved senses (i.e. the temporal cortex for the auditory stimulation) to the occipital cortex deprived of its most salient visual input.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the results

claim: The increased representation of sound categories in the VOTC of EB and LB people could be an extension of the intrinsic multisensory categorical organization of the VOTC, that is therefore partially independent from vision in sighted as well.
source: This has broad implications since it supports the idea that the increased representation of sound categories in the VOTC of EB and LB people could be an extension of the intrinsic multisensory categorical organization of the VOTC, that is therefore partially independent from vision in sighted as well (Mattioni et al., 2020; see also Amedi et al., 2002; Ricciardi and Pietrini, 2011; Striem-Amit and Amedi, 2014).
evidence: Interpretation supported by current results and citations to previous work

claim: In all the groups (i.e. SC, EB, and LB) a big portion of the temporal cortex (including the superior temporal gyrus [STG], part of the middle temporal gyrus, and the Heschl gyrus both in the left and in the right hemispheres) show a highly significant stability of the patterns.
source: Our data show that in all the groups (i.e. SC, EB, and LB) a big portion of the temporal cortex (including the superior temporal gyrus [STG], part of the middle temporal gyrus, and the Heschl gyrus both in the left and in the right hemispheres) show a highly significant stability of the patterns, suggesting that these portions of the temporal cortex have a stable representation of the sounds we selected.
evidence: Supported by split-half analysis presented in supplementary figure

claim: The split-half correlation is increased in the occipital cortex of both EB and LB groups compared to the SC.
source: Interestingly, we also observed that the split-half correlation is increased in the occipital cortex of both EB and LB groups compared to the SC and it is, concomitantly, decreased in the temporal cortex of both blind groups (EB and LB) when compared to sighted subjects.
evidence: Supported by split-half analysis presented in supplementary figure

claim: The split-half correlation is decreased in the temporal cortex of both blind groups (EB and LB) when compared to sighted subjects.
source: Interestingly, we also observed that the split-half correlation is increased in the occipital cortex of both EB and LB groups compared to the SC and it is, concomitantly, decreased in the temporal cortex of both blind groups (EB and LB) when compared to sighted subjects.
evidence: Supported by split-half analysis presented in supplementary figure

claim: Models of some acoustic features of sounds (pitch, HNR) correlate more with the representational structure implemented in the Heschl gyrus (pitch) and in a specific portion of the right STS (HNR).
source: Importantly, we additionally show how our stimuli are well suited to address such question (Figure 6) by demonstrating, in all groups, that models of some acoustic features of our sounds (pitch, HNR) correlate more with the representational structure implemented in the Heschl gyrus (pitch) and in a specific portion of the right STS (HNR) while the 'human' model correlates more with the representational structure of an extended bilateral portion of STS (see also Giordano et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by RSA with partial correlation analysis shown in Figure 6

claim: The 'human' model correlates more with the representational structure of an extended bilateral portion of STS.
source: Importantly, we additionally show how our stimuli are well suited to address such question (Figure 6) by demonstrating, in all groups, that models of some acoustic features of our sounds (pitch, HNR) correlate more with the representational structure implemented in the Heschl gyrus (pitch) and in a specific portion of the right STS (HNR) while the 'human' model correlates more with the representational structure of an extended bilateral portion of STS (see also Giordano et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by RSA with partial correlation analysis shown in Figure 6 and citation to Giordano et al., 2013

claim: Acoustic features of sound processing are not altered in the auditory region and not represented in the occipital cortex of EB and LB people.
source: It shows for the first time that acoustic features of sound processing are not altered in the auditory region and not represented in the occipital cortex of EB and LB people.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from RSA analysis with acoustic models

claim: The representation of a higher-level category 'Human/Voice' is reduced in temporal regions and enhanced in occipital regions.
source: In contrast, the representation of a higher-level category 'Human/Voice' is reduced in temporal regions and enhanced in occipital regions (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by RSA analysis with human model shown in Figure 4B

claim: The same feature of sounds is concomitantly reorganized in temporal and occipital cortices of both blind groups.
source: Showing that the same feature of our sounds is concomitantly reorganized in temporal and occipital cortices of both blind groups is filling in an important gap in the literature about how changes in the deprived and remaining senses relate to each other in case of early and late visual deprivation, providing a mechanistic view on the way plasticity expresses following blindness.
evidence: Interpretation of the results showing coordinated reorganization

claim: Enhanced decoding accuracies in the occipital ROI of EB when compared to SC was concomitant to reduced decoding accuracy in the temporal cortex of EB people.
source: Results from the eight-way MVP classification analysis show enhanced decoding accuracies in the occipital ROI of EB when compared to SC that was concomitant to reduced decoding accuracy in the temporal cortex of EB people (see Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by MVPA decoding analysis shown in Figure 3

claim: LB showed enhanced representation of sound categories in the occipital ROI compared to SC while the temporal cortex showed lower decoding in LB.
source: Like what was observed in EB, LB also showed enhanced representation of sound categories in the occipital ROI compared to SC while the temporal cortex showed lower decoding in LB.
evidence: Supported by MVPA decoding analysis

claim: The reorganization of occipital regions is less functionally organized in late blindness than the one observed in early blindness according to a dominant view in the field.
source: A dominant view in the field is that the reorganization of occipital regions is less functionally organized in late blindness than the one observed in early blindness (Bedny et al., 2012; Collignon et al., 2013; Kanjlia et al., 2009).
evidence: Describes a view from previous literature supported by citations

claim: The current study's results overturn the view that reorganization of occipital regions is less functionally organized in late blindness by showing functionally specific coding of sound categories that is present in LB and increased compared to SC.
source: Our results overturn this view by showing functionally specific coding of sound categories that is present in LB and increased compared to SC (see Figure 3A and Appendix 1).
evidence: Interpretation of current results in contrast to previous literature

claim: Within each blind subject, the correlation between the occipital and the temporal categorical representations is significantly higher compared to the SC.
source: Our results suggest that this is indeed the case. In fact we show that within each blind subject, the correlation between the occipital and the temporal categorical representations is significantly higher compared to the SC (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by RSA correlation analysis shown in Figure 4A

claim: In every group the best model for temporal cortex was a 'human' model, in which human stimuli were considered similar between themselves and different from all other animate and inanimate stimuli.
source: In the temporal cortex, we found that in every group the best model was a 'human' model, in which human stimuli were considered similar between themselves and different from all other animate and inanimate stimuli (Figure 5A and C).
evidence: Supported by RSA analysis with representational models shown in Figure 5

claim: The two occipital ROIs are located within the fusiform gyrus/infero-temporal cortex, partially overlapping with the fusiform face area.
source: This finding is well compatible with the spatial location of our ROIs which correspond to regions known to be involved in the processing of faces and voices, respectively (Benetti et al., 2017). Indeed, the two occipital ROIs are located within the fusiform gyrus/infero-temporal cortex, partially overlapping with the fusiform face area (Julian et al., 2009), while the two temporal ROIs are located within the STG, extending over the left and right temporal voice area (Belin et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by anatomical localization and citations

claim: The two temporal ROIs are located within the STG, extending over the left and right temporal voice area.
source: This finding is well compatible with the spatial location of our ROIs which correspond to regions known to be involved in the processing of faces and voices, respectively (Benetti et al., 2017). Indeed, the two occipital ROIs are located within the fusiform gyrus/infero-temporal cortex, partially overlapping with the fusiform face area (Julian et al., 2009), while the two temporal ROIs are located within the STG, extending over the left and right temporal voice area (Belin et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by anatomical localization and citations

claim: It is only the representational structure of the 'human' model that is reduced in both LB and EB groups in temporal regions, but not the encoding of other categorical and low-level acoustic features which is similar across groups.
source: We also show that it is only the representational structure of our 'human' model that is reduced in both LB and EB groups in temporal regions, but not the encoding of other categorical and low-level acoustic features which is similar across groups (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by RSA analysis with multiple models shown in Figure 5C

claim: There is enhanced representation of the 'human' model in EB and LB people in occipital regions but no alteration in the representation of other categorical or acoustic features of the sounds.
source: Interestingly, this result relates to the reversed group difference observed in the occipital regions where we find enhanced representation of the 'human' model in EB and LB people but no alteration in the representation of other categorical or acoustic features of the sounds (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by RSA analysis with multiple models shown in Figure 5D
